description: OrbitSense is a solo team focused on applying artificial intelligence, computer vision, and data analysis to planetary exploration.
summary: OrbitSense is an interactive tool for comparing Earth terrain with selected areas near Shackleton Crater on the Moon and Jezero Crater on Mars. It uses NASADEM, LOLA and MOLA elevation observations to measure slope, roughness and relative relief on a common 800 m grid. The current catalogue contains ten Earth candidates and three comparison controls. Users can explore the sites on a map, adjust feature weights, inspect measurements and sources, and download results. Cima Volcanic Field ranks highest for the Jezero reference under equal weights. The selected catalogue shows weak agreement with the lunar reference. Evaluation compares the method with a baseline based on relief alone and tests changes in weights, window size and grid resolution. OrbitSense supports preliminary selection of field settings for exploration research through transparent comparisons and documented limits.
details:
OrbitSense compares Earth terrain with defined areas near Shackleton Crater on the Moon and Jezero Crater on Mars. It supports the initial selection of field settings for exploration research. Users can select a planetary reference, inspect Earth sites on a map, change feature weights, compare measurements, and download results in CSV or JSON format.

The catalogue contains ten Earth candidates and three comparison controls. The lunar reference is a 25.6 km square centred at 89.67 degrees south and 129.78 degrees east. It includes crater, rim and exterior terrain near Shackleton. The Martian reference is a square of the same size centred at 18.4447 degrees north and 77.4508 degrees east near Jezero’s western floor. Both references contain several landform units. Saved polygons and local azimuthal equidistant coordinate definitions document their exact footprints.

Earth elevations come from NASADEM HGT v001. All selected Earth windows fall within its coverage. The lunar reference uses the adjusted 80 m LOLA south polar elevation product. Mars elevations come from the MGS MOLA global model with nominal 463 m sampling. Source records identify the products, access routes, acquisition information, coordinate systems and crop checksums.

Python preprocessing transforms each location to an appropriate local metric grid and averages elevation into 800 m cells before calculating terrain descriptors. The method measures median slope in degrees, root mean square elevation residual after removing a fitted plane in metres, and relative relief in metres. Relative relief is the difference between the 95th and 5th elevation percentiles. Missing observations and affected gradients are excluded. A window needs at least 95 percent valid elevation cells and a complete feature vector to receive a score.

Descriptor similarity decreases exponentially with the absolute difference from the reference, scaled by a declared tolerance. The score is 100 times the weighted mean of these similarities. Tolerances use reference variability across measured perturbations, with minimum scales of 1 degree for slope, 100 m for roughness and 250 m for relief. The interface displays the tolerances and each descriptor’s contribution.

With equal weights, Cima Volcanic Field ranks first for Jezero at 63.78, followed by El Pinacate at 52.59 and Atacama Yungay at 46.59. Shackleton gives weak agreement across this catalogue. The Himalaya control ranks first at 15.87, while Mauna Kea has the highest candidate score at 1.73.

Evaluation includes 200 Dirichlet weight draws and seven measured variants of window size, position and grid resolution. A baseline using relative relief alone returns the same top three sites as the full method for both targets. A 19.2 km window changes one member of each shortlist. These findings show how analytical choices affect the results. Documented analog relationships provide separate geological or environmental context for selected locations.

The project combines reproducible observations with adjustable rankings and traceable explanations. It can help researchers compare possible field settings and help educators explain how an analogy depends on the property being studied. Python, NumPy, Rasterio, GDAL, pyproj, Requests and Pillow support processing. HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Leaflet provide the interface, with an OpenStreetMap basemap. Flask supports integration with the portfolio website. Saved feature files keep browser calculations lightweight.

The catalogue is a selected sample, and the measurements describe regional terrain. Vegetation, structures, source age and interpolated elevation affect interpretation. Material composition, illumination, habitability, landing safety and local mobility require separate evidence. Finer observations and mapped geological units would support more detailed comparisons.
